caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Ghana's debt cycle is the continent's most dramatic boom-bust. From 17.3% of GDP in 2006 (post-HIPC), election-cycle spending, energy debts, and Eurobond borrowing drove it to 92.7% by 2022, the series high. In December 2022 Ghana defaulted on external debt, the first major COVID-era African default after Zambia. The May 2023 IMF Extended Credit Facility ($3 billion) anchored a restructuring: domestic debt exchange, then external creditor deals, cut the ratio to a projected 48.9% in 2025. The speed of the decline reflects restructuring haircuts and cedi stabilization as much as consolidation; sustainability now depends on staying out of the election-spending trap that caused three previous IMF programs.
inflation_management: Ghana's inflation targeting regime (formal target 8±2%) has been repeatedly overwhelmed by fiscal dominance and cedi depreciation. Inflation ran at 10-17% through the 2010s, peaking at 17.5% in 2016, before the central bank brought it to 7.2% by 2019, the best performance in years. The 2022 crisis destroyed that progress: the cedi collapsed and inflation surged to 31.9% in 2022 and a series high of 39.2% in 2023. Aggressive tightening (policy rate to 30%) and the IMF program broke the spiral: 22.9% in 2024 and a projected 14.2% in 2025. The Bank of Ghana's credibility is slowly being rebuilt, but markets will judge it by the next election cycle, not the current disinflation.

key_events.event: Oil production began at Jubilee field, adding a new revenue stream.
Power crisis ('dumsor') and fiscal slippages; IMF program (2015) stabilized the economy.
COVID-19 and election-year spending pushed debt toward 90% of GDP.
December 2022: sovereign default on external debt; cedi collapsed; inflation hit 54% year-on-year at year-end.
May 17, 2023: IMF approved a $3 billion Extended Credit Facility; debt restructuring began.
December 2024: John Mahama won the presidency, returning to power as the IMF program neared completion.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued IMF-anchored recovery: inflation back to single digits, debt near 50% of GDP, and gold/oil revenues supporting the cedi. Upside comes from the restructuring's clean slate and the 2024 political reset; downside is Ghana's history, four IMF programs in fifteen years, each undone by election spending. Uncertainty is moderate: the institutions are stronger than in 2022, but the test is whether fiscal discipline survives the next election.
